title: Geometric orbit lifting through a finite normal scalar extension
statement:
Let $e\subseteq F\subseteq K$ be fields with $K/e$ finite and normal: every minimal polynomial over $e$ of an element of $K$ splits into linear factors in $K[T]$. Let $J$ and $\Gamma$ be finite groups, let $\rho:J\to\operatorname{Aut}_e(F)$, $r:\Gamma\twoheadrightarrow J$, and $\alpha:\Gamma\to\operatorname{Aut}_e(K)$ be homomorphisms such that $\alpha(\gamma)|_F=\rho(r(\gamma))$ and
$$\alpha(\ker r)=\operatorname{Aut}_F(K).$$
Let $V$ be a finite-type $F$-scheme with a left $J$-action semilinear for $\rho$, using the convention that $j$ acts on $\operatorname{Spec}F$ by $\operatorname{Spec}(\rho(j)^{-1})$. Let $B$ be an $e$-scheme and $v:V\to B$ a $J$-invariant $e$-morphism. Put $W=V\times_F K$ and give $W$ the diagonal $\Gamma$-action from $r$ on $V$ and $\alpha$ on $K$. For every geometric point $b:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to B$, where $\Omega$ is algebraically closed, put $V_b=V\times_B\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ and $W_b=W\times_B\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$. If the underlying points of $V_b$ form a nonempty single $J$-orbit, then every point $x\in V_b$ is $\Omega$-rational, meaning its structural residue map $\Omega\to\kappa(x)$ is an isomorphism. For each such $x$, the points of the fibre of $W_b\to V_b$ over $x$ identify with the field embeddings $\beta:K\hookrightarrow\Omega$ extending the scalar map $F\to\Omega$ of $x$, by the evaluation maps $\Omega\otimes_{F,x}K\to\Omega$, $z\otimes k\mapsto z\beta(k)$. This set is nonempty. For $\gamma\in\ker r$, its action on these embeddings is $\beta\mapsto\beta\circ\alpha(\gamma)^{-1}$. The underlying points of $W_b$ form a nonempty single $\Gamma$-orbit. No separability, reducedness, faithfulness of either action, or normality of $F/e$ is assumed. Fields and finite extensions use [def-weil-field], [def-pc-field-extension], [def-pc-field-tower]; schemes, finite type, fibre products, geometric points and residue fields use [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-weil-geometric-point], [def-weil-residue-field].

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.150, geometric-orbit clause for (2.b); agent elaboration, former steps 7–8 of lem-sfb-common-field-semilinear-induction. proof.text: First $v$ is locally of finite type, even though $B$ is arbitrary. For an affine open $T=\operatorname{Spec}R\subset B$ and an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subset v^{-1}(T)$, [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs] applied to $V\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ makes $A$ a finitely generated $F$-algebra. Since $F/e$ is finite (an $e$-linearly independent subset of $F$ remains one in the finite-dimensional $e$-space $K$), an $e$-basis of $F$, together with these algebra generators, generates $A$ as an $e$-algebra. The same elements generate $A$ over $R$, because $e\to A$ factors through $R$. Applying the affine-pairs criterion to $v$ and then [lem-weil-pbc-lft-base-change] shows that $V_b\to\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is locally of finite type. Only local finite type, not quasi-compactness of $v$, is needed.

The finite group $J$ acts transitively on the nonempty set $|V_b|$, so this set is finite. A scheme is $T_0$: if two points specialize to each other, an affine open containing either contains both, since opens are stable under generization. On that affine, specialization means inclusion of prime ideals (the closure of $\{\mathfrak p\}$ is $V(\mathfrak p)$), so mutual specialization gives equality [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Among the finitely many nonempty point closures choose one minimal under inclusion, say $\overline{\{x_0\}}$. If $y$ lies in it, then $\overline{\{y\}}\subseteq\overline{\{x_0\}}$, so minimality and $T_0$ give $y=x_0$. Thus $x_0$ is closed. Each $j$ acts by a homeomorphism, so transitivity makes every point closed. The closed-point residue theorem [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base], applied to the locally finite-type $\Omega$-scheme from step 1, now gives the structural isomorphism $\Omega\xrightarrow{\sim}\kappa(x)$ for every $x$.

source.place: Tag 00FV (theorem-nullstellensatz (1)); closed-point consequence as stated in lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base; finite T0 argument written out

proof.text: The universal property [def-pc-fibre-product] identifies $W_b$ with $V_b\times_{\operatorname{Spec}F}\operatorname{Spec}K$, compatibly with its projection and the diagonal action: both objects parameterize a map to $V$, a map to $\operatorname{Spec}K$ agreeing over $F$, and a map to $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ agreeing over $B$. Fix $x\in V_b$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-points], the points over $x$ identify with the primes of $\kappa(x)\otimes_F K=\Omega\otimes_{F,x}K=:A_x$, using the structural isomorphism of step 2. Equivalently, pulling back further to $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$ gives the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A_x$ by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra].

source.place: Tags 01JT (lemma-points-fibre-product), 01I4 (lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes); associativity verified by universal property

proof.text: Choose a finite $F$-basis $(k_i)$ of $K$; such a basis exists since an $F$-linearly independent set in $K$ is $e$-linearly independent. The elements $1\otimes k_i$ span $A_x$ over $\Omega$: expand each $k$ in that basis and use the balancing relation. Thus for any prime $\mathfrak p\subset A_x$, the domain $D=A_x/\mathfrak p$ is a finite-dimensional $\Omega$-vector space. For $0\ne d\in D$, multiplication by $d$ is an injective linear endomorphism and hence surjective, so $D$ is a field. Linear dependence of $1,d,d^2,\ldots$ makes every $d$ algebraic over $\Omega$. Applying [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-over-algebraically-closed-subfield] shows that the structural map $\Omega\to D$ is surjective, and it is injective because $D$ is a nonzero field. Therefore it is an isomorphism. This argument allows nilpotents in $A_x$.

For each prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A_x$, compose $A_x\to A_x/\mathfrak p$ with the inverse of the structural isomorphism in step 4 to obtain an $\Omega$-algebra homomorphism $q:A_x\to\Omega$. Its restriction $\beta(k)=q(1\otimes k)$ is a unital field homomorphism $K\hookrightarrow\Omega$ extending the scalar map of $x$, and $q(z\otimes k)=z\beta(k)$. Conversely this evaluation formula is balanced over $F$, additive and multiplicative, so any such embedding defines a surjective homomorphism with prime kernel. These constructions are inverse: a homomorphism to $\Omega$ with a given kernel is unique since the induced map from $A_x/\mathfrak p$, already equal to $\Omega$ through its structural map, is forced to be its inverse. Finally [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-extension-embeds-algebraically-closed] applies to the algebraic extension $K/F$ and the scalar embedding $F\to\Omega$, giving an embedding $\beta$ and therefore a point over every $x$.

source.place: Tag 09GU (lemma-map-into-algebraic-closure); tensor evaluation and kernel inverse written out

proof.text: Let $\gamma\in\ker r$. It acts identically on $V_b$, including the residue field at $x$, and on the scalar factor by $\operatorname{Spec}(\alpha(\gamma)^{-1})$. Consequently on $A_x$ its pullback is $z\otimes k\mapsto z\otimes\alpha(\gamma)^{-1}(k)$. For the point with evaluation $q_\beta$, its image has prime kernel equal to that of $q_\beta$ composed with this pullback. On a pure tensor this composite is $z\beta(\alpha(\gamma)^{-1}(k))$, so step 5 identifies its embedding with $\beta\circ\alpha(\gamma)^{-1}$, as asserted. The inverse in this formula is required by the given left-action convention; the $\Omega$ factor is fixed because the action is taken over $b$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.150, diagram (2.b); agent computation from the specified action convention

proof.text: The finite degree of $K/e$ makes each $k\in K$ algebraic over $e$: the powers $1,k,\ldots,k^{[K:e]}$ are linearly dependent. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-normal-extension-normal-over-intermediate] applies to $e\subseteq F\subseteq K$ and makes $K/F$ algebraic normal, with no separability required. Fix $x$ and two of its embeddings $\beta_1,\beta_2$. The existing normal-embedding lemma [lem-sfb-normal-embeddings-automorphism-transitive] gives $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}_F(K)$ with $\beta_2=\beta_1\circ\sigma$. The hypothesis $\alpha(\ker r)=\operatorname{Aut}_F(K)$ supplies $\gamma\in\ker r$ with $\alpha(\gamma)=\sigma^{-1}$. Step 6 then shows that $\gamma$ carries the point of $\beta_1$ to the point of $\beta_2$. Thus the kernel is transitive on each nonempty scalar fibre.

There is a point of $W_b$ by nonemptiness of $V_b$ and step 5. Given $y_1,y_2\in W_b$, write $x_i$ for their projections. Choose $j\in J$ with $jx_1=x_2$ and choose $\delta\in\Gamma$ with $r(\delta)=j$. The diagonal projection is equivariant, so $\delta y_1$ and $y_2$ lie over $x_2$. By step 7 some $\gamma\in\ker r$ satisfies $\gamma\delta y_1=y_2$. Hence all points form a single $\Gamma$-orbit. Every construction used only normality and finite degree, and all arguments concerned prime kernels rather than a reduced or separable tensor decomposition; no faithfulness or normality of $F/e$ was used.
